# Satapattajātaka (Ja 279)

**ID:** Ja 279
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Satapattajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Woodpecker
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja279

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Satapattajātaka* (Ja 279), translated by Bhikkhu Sujato as *The Woodpecker*, is a canonical verse narrative located in the Jātaka collection of the Pali canon [SuttaCentral]. The commentary notes that the Buddha delivered this teaching while residing at the Jetavana monastery in Sāvatthi regarding the monks Paṇḍuka and Lohita, two members of the contentious "group of six" (*chabbaggiyā*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879; Horner, Cullavagga]. The canonical verses begin with the incipit *Yathā māṇavako panthe* ("As the youth upon his way") [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. In the story's resolution (*samodhāna*), the Buddha reveals that he himself was the leader of the bandits in that previous life [Fausböll 1879].

In the narrative of the past, the Bodhisatta lived as the chief of a gang of five hundred robbers who sustained themselves through highway robbery and housebreaking [Law 1926; Chen 2015]. Despite this vocation, he is portrayed as a good robber who correctly interprets omens for an oncoming traveler and lets him continue his journey with his belongings intact [Appleton 2010]. Scholars note that the commentary explains this rare flawed incarnation—one of only two instances where the Bodhisatta is reborn as a bandit—as being beyond his moral control, attributing his criminal livelihood to an astrological defect in his horoscope rather than an ethical failing [Chen 2015; Appleton 2010].

SuttaCentral does not record any curated cross-language parallels for the text [SuttaCentral]. Algorithmic text-reuse analysis via DharmaNexus also identified no cross-language matches scoring 10 or above, but confirmed internal Pali reuse between Ja 279 and the commentary (*Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, Dutiyo bhāgo) spanning three matches, the longest aligning segments §1.1–3.4 with commentary units §2504–2512 [DharmaNexus].
